title: Empirical Autoscale Labbook — Dedicated Pools
body:
Purpose:
This is a working labbook to capture reproducible experiments and pragmatic knobs for autoscaling dedicated GPU pools. Aim: move beyond policy sketches to an empirically validated set of autoscale parameters, warm-pool sizing heuristics, and isolation toggles that operations can apply with predictable latency and cost outcomes.

Context and motivation:
- We have many high-level PRDs with strategies (credit pools, lane tiers, soft-eviction) but limited empirical signals about how parameter choices interact with real model workloads (kv cache warmup, long-tail sequence lengths, multi-tenant concurrency).
- This document collects controlled experiments, the harness configs, and short-run conclusions we can immediately productize or operationalize.

Experiment methodology (explicit so reproducible):
- Harness: scale-tests repo (link above). Tests run against a dedicated-staging cluster (small heterogeneous GPU fleet) using the same serving runtime used in prod.
- Workload families: 
  * chat-burst (conversations with frequent short messages, mean 40 tokens, 95th 512)
  * long-infer (single long prompt heavy KV reuse; mean 1,200 tokens)
  * embedding-spike (many short requests parallel)
  * mixed-prod (traffic shape sampled from anonymized 3-day trace of customer X)
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p99 tail latency (endpoint and token-level), successful token throughput, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate, cold-warm handoff time, cost-per-token (estimated).
- Repetition: each experiment runs 3 independent trials at fixed seeds; we report median results and show run variance in artifacts folder (artifact file names referenced in linked_artifacts).

Key experiments and highlights (short):
1) Warm-pool sizing vs coldstart latency:
- Setup: 0, 1, 2, 4 warm workers per rack. Measured cold->warm median token latency and p99.
- Result: adding 1 warm worker reduces median cold token latency by ~37% and p99 by ~24% for chat-burst; diminishing returns after 2 workers. For long-infer, benefits persist longer due to larger KV footprint.
- Ops implication: default warm-pool = 1 per shard; increase to 2 for models with >1k seq median or customer-specified latency tiers.

2) Autoscale window and smoothing parameters (observe, commit, decay):
- Tested short observe window (15s), medium (60s), long (300s) with commit thresholds tuned for throughput change.
- Short windows react faster but cause oscillation for spiky workloads (embedding-spike). 60s provides a good tradeoff; 300s too slow for customer-critical spikes.
- Recommendation: default observe=60s, commit threshold = +25% sustained utilization, decay half-life ~10 minutes for graceful downscale. Provide per-customer overrides.

3) Soft-eviction vs hard-eviction when pool saturation occurs:
- Soft-evict (reduce concurrency per-tenant + degrade fidelity lane) reduces p99 by up to 18% for remaining tenants versus hard eviction which preserves p50 but causes abrupt errors for evicted tenants.
- For SLA-backed tenants, prefer controlled hard-evict with preflight notifications; for self-serve prefer soft-evict.

4) Affinity and topology-aware placement:
- Placing warm workers for high-KV models on same rack decreased inter-node KV rehydrate time by ~30ms median and improved p99 tail by ~10% in hybrid long-infer workloads.
- Recommendation: add a topology affinity tag for pinned reserved slots.

5) Burst-credit ledger simulation (micro-provisioning spiking customers):
- Simulated customers consuming burst credits; naive immediate replenishment led to synchronized spikes causing global contention. Sharded replenishment (randomized replenishment windows) smoothed load and reduced cascade failures.

Notes on failure modes observed:
- KV cache eviction storms: when multiple large models deallocate, downstream tenants suffer large p99 spikes due to cache churn. Mitigation: staggered cache eviction and persistence hints for frequently reused prefixes.
- Autoscale chase: aggressive vertical scale-up when sample is noisy; solution: add hysteresis and require two consecutive windows above threshold before scaling up.
- Cold worker GPU TTFB variance: observed non-deterministic driver warm times on older GPU types; protect by conservative warm counts per older hardware.

Operational playbook (runbook snippets):
- Incident: p99 spike across pool with low GPU utilization -> check KV cache hit rate; if hit rate drop then run cache-resim (resim script) and enable staged-cache-repopulate (script name).
- Rapid surge: if observed throughput > 2x baseline and queue growing, enable ephemeral warm-up lanes (operator toggle) which preempt opportunistic idle GPUs for 5–15 minutes.
- Eviction policy switch: toggle soft-evict for non-enterprise customers; hard-evict with pre-warning buffer for enterprise (policy id: P-DED-HARD-1).

Product knobs to ship (concrete):
- warm_workers_per_shard (int), default 1; allow per-model override and per-customer skin.
- observe_window_seconds (default 60), commit_threshold_percent (default 25), downscale_half_life_seconds (default 600).
- soft_evict_enabled_by_default (bool) for tier=free/standard customers.
- burst_replenish_jitter_ms (default 30000) to randomize credit replenishment.
- topology_affinity_tagging (enum) with options none/rack/zone.

Unresolved questions / follow-ups (experiments to run):
- Measure long-run cost delta of keeping a small global warm pool vs many per-shard warm workers for multi-model fleets (1–2 week runs).
- Quantify interaction of quantized model variants (8-bit) with warm-pool behavior — does quantization reduce warm overhead enough to change warm_worker defaults?
- Evaluate client-perceived quality when soft-evict steers tenants to lower-fidelity models during surge — measure semantic degradation with small eval sets.

Artifacts & reproducibility notes:
- All harness configs in github.com/redwood-inference/scale-tests under /experiments/labbook-2025. Run script: tools/run-lab-experiment.sh --suite labbook-2025 --artifact-dir /tmp/out
- Raw telemetry snapshots saved to s3://redwood-int/scale-labbook/2025-11-*

Appendix (short):
- Quick comparison table (observational):
  * Warm pool 0 -> 1: big wins for chat; long-infer still benefits from 2+
  * observe 15s: fast but oscillates; 60s: balanced; 300s: slow reaction

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic: the goal is to converge on a small set of conservative defaults we can ship in the next SRE/Platform tick. Reviewers: pls run the linked reproducibility scripts in your own staging clusters and paste results back into this doc under a new section named "validation-<yourname>-2026".
- If you want a shorter PRD, I can distill this into a 2-page decision doc listing only the knobs and final recommended defaults.

Raw experimental outputs and visual graphs are attached in the artifacts bucket; see linked_artifacts for pointers.

Open questions for product direction (vote on one):
- A: Ship conservative defaults + per-tenant overrides (favored)
- B: Ship aggressive defaults tuned for PLG growth (risk of oscillation)
- C: Expose full knobs to self-serve and keep platform defaults minimal

End of labbook (working).
